rationale: The strongest CRC signal in Baxter-type data comes from a small group of oral pathobionts (Fusobacterium, Porphyromonas, Parvimonas, Peptostreptococcus, Gemella and similar). Each is sparse in any one sample, so the random forest rarely splits on them usefully. I'm adding label-free features built from taxonomy names: the summed abundance of these markers and how many of them are present. These are denser, more reliable features than the individual genera, and they work the same way on other studies.

Many of the ~200+ genera are present in only a handful of samples. They are mostly sequencing noise, and they take up the random forest's sqrt(p) candidate features at each split, which crowds out the informative taxa. I'm dropping genera found in fewer than 10% of training samples. This filter only looks at whether a genus is present, never at labels, and it is computed inside each training fold; the aggregate marker features are always kept.

Colorectal cancer stool shows two linked shifts: oral pathobionts go up and butyrate-producing commensals (Faecalibacterium, Roseburia, Coprococcus and similar) go down. A random forest can only split on one feature at a time, so it can't easily use the ratio between these two groups. I'm adding log-ratio balance features (oral-marker sum against butyrate-producer sum), built only from taxonomy names, as a depth-independent CRC index. It should also carry over to the other four CRC studies.

I'm adding a second model and averaging the two by rank. The random forest uses raw relative abundances; the new model is an L2 logistic regression on log-transformed genera. The CRC signal is spread across many modest log-scale shifts (more oral pathobionts, fewer butyrate producers), which a linear model on log abundances picks up well and an RF on 292 samples only captures approximately. The two models make different errors, so averaging them should raise AUROC. Only the logistic model drops genera present in fewer than 10% of training samples, and its regularization strength is chosen by inner grouped CV on the training fold. The RF is unchanged.

Right now every OTU without a genus assignment is merged into one shared `g__` column. That column mixes unrelated taxa, such as unclassified Lachnospiraceae and Ruminococcaceae (butyrate producers that drop in CRC) and unclassified Enterobacteriaceae (which tend to rise). I'm giving each unclassified OTU the name of its deepest known rank instead (for example `f__Lachnospiraceae;g__unclassified`). That keeps these large, informative groups separate for both models, and since the names come from taxonomy rather than study-specific OTU ids, they carry over to the other CRC studies.

The logistic model currently gives every zero the same pseudocount (5e-5). But a zero in a 3,000-read sample means much less than a zero in a 60,000-read sample, because the shallow sample may simply have missed the genus. I'm switching to a pseudocount of half a read, log((count + 0.5) / depth), so each imputed zero sits at that sample's own detection limit. This should stop sequencing depth from leaking into the log-abundance features. The random forest is unchanged, and the change uses only within-sample read totals, so it applies the same way to the other studies.

I'm adding family-level log-abundances alongside the genus features, for the logistic model only. CRC's loss of butyrate producers is spread across many sparse Lachnospiraceae and Ruminococcaceae genera, and the rise in oral pathobionts spans whole families (Porphyromonadaceae, Fusobacteriaceae, Peptostreptococcaceae). Family totals are denser and less noisy than any single genus, and they are built from taxonomy names, so they carry over to the other studies. The random forest keeps its current inputs, because round 5 showed that adding columns to it hurt.

The logistic model gets four alpha-diversity features computed per sample: OTU Shannon entropy, log inverse-Simpson, genus-level Shannon, and log expected richness at a fixed depth of 1,000 reads. Expected richness is calculated exactly rather than by random subsampling, so it is deterministic and does not depend on sequencing depth. CRC stool tends to lose many low-abundance commensals and to be dominated by fewer taxa, and the individual taxon log-abundances don't capture that community-wide shift. The random forest keeps its current inputs, because extra columns have hurt it before.

I'm adding a third model to the rank-average: CatBoost with shallow, strongly regularized trees, trained on the full multi-resolution feature set (genera, families, alpha-diversity and the marker aggregates). The random forest only sees genera and the logistic model only sees additive log-scale effects. Boosting can pick up threshold-type interactions between them, such as oral pathobionts appearing together with low diversity, and its errors should differ from the other two models. All three models get equal weight.

The forest is currently fully grown (min_samples_leaf=1). With 292 noisy, zero-inflated samples, that gives jagged probability estimates and hurts the ranking AUROC depends on. I'm choosing the leaf size (1/3/5/10) on each training fold by out-of-bag AUROC, which uses only training data, so the forest can smooth its votes when that helps. Everything else stays the same.

Relative abundances are compositional, so when one taxon blooms (for example an oral pathobiont) every other taxon's share drops, even if its absolute level hasn't changed. This change applies a centered log-ratio (CLR) transform to the logistic model's inputs. Each sample's log-abundances are centred on that sample's mean log-abundance, done separately for genera and for families, so the model sees each taxon's level relative to the rest of the community instead of these artefacts. It uses only within-sample values and taxonomy names, so it transfers to the other CRC studies; the random forest is unchanged.

With a pseudocount of 5e-5, a genus going from absent to a single read only moves the logistic model's feature by about 0.3 log10 units. Yet for sparse oral pathobionts and lost commensals in CRC, whether the genus is detected at all is often the main signal. I'm adding hurdle-style presence/absence indicators to the logistic model only, for genera present in 10–90% of training samples, so detection and abundance are modelled separately.

This round changes only the logistic model's penalty. It moves from pure L2 to elastic net, and inner grouped CV on each training fold picks the mix (l1_ratio from 0 to 0.75) along with the regularization strength. The CRC signal comes mostly from a few sparse oral pathobiont markers plus a handful of groups of butyrate producers, so a partly sparse model should cut noise from the ~300 correlated genus, family and diversity features. Because 0 (pure L2) stays one of the options, the inner CV can keep the current setup on any fold where sparsity doesn't help.

I'm adding co-abundance group (CAG) features, for the logistic model only. In featurize, genera present in at least 10% of samples are clustered by Spearman correlation of their log-abundances (average linkage, mean ρ > 0.3, no labels used). Each sample then gets the summed abundance of every multi-genus cluster. CRC signal comes from guilds that span families, such as oral pathobionts that occur together and butyrate producers that are lost together. Taxonomy-based family totals cannot capture these groups, and the clusters are rebuilt from taxonomy names on each study, so they transfer to the other CRC studies.

I'm replacing the random forest with ExtraTrees trained on log10 genus abundances, keeping the marker features unchanged. Relative abundances are zero-inflated and heavy-tailed. ExtraTrees picks split thresholds at random, uniformly between each feature's min and max, so on a log scale those thresholds cover the multiplicative range where CRC shifts actually happen. On the raw scale they would mostly fall in the long upper tail. Averaging random splits should also give smoother rankings than a fully grown random forest on just 292 samples.

Adding family-level totals helped the logistic model (round 7). This round adds order- and class-level log-abundances to the logistic model only, because some CRC shifts show up at those higher ranks. Examples are Clostridiales butyrate producers against Bacteroidales, and Fusobacteriia or Bacilli/Gemellales oral taxa. Totals at these ranks are denser and less noisy than family or genus totals, and they are built from taxonomy names, so they carry over to the other CRC studies. The random forest inputs don't change, since adding columns to it has hurt before.

The logistic model picks its L2 strength from a single 5-fold inner CV on about 230 training samples, so the selection is noisy, and a badly chosen C on some folds may be dragging the ensemble down. I'm switching that selection to 3 repeats of 5-fold StratifiedGroupKFold with fixed seeds, which averages AUROC over 15 class-balanced folds and should give a steadier choice of regularization; nothing else changes.

Right now the random forest and the logistic model are averaged 50/50, but the logistic model is probably the stronger one (adding it gave +0.025). This change picks the blend weight on each training fold instead. The forest's out-of-bag predictions and nested grouped-CV predictions from the logistic model are scored by AUROC, and the best weight in {0.2, 0.35, 0.5, 0.65, 0.8} is used. Both models always contribute, and neither model's features nor settings change.
